entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Radegund (c. 520–587), a Thuringian princess by birth and a Frankish queen by forced marriage to Chlothar I, stands as a pivotal figure in early medieval European history, particularly for her pioneering role in establishing one of the most significant female monastic houses of the era, the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers. Her life, marked by political upheaval, personal piety, and intellectual pursuits, exemplifies the complex interplay of secular power, religious devotion, and female agency within the Merovingian world. Radegund's foundation not only offered a sanctuary for women but also became a vibrant center for learning and the arts, fostering the transmission of Christian culture and serving as a beacon of spiritual authority in sixth-century Gaul.

Born into the Thuringian royal family around 520, Radegund's destiny was irrevocably altered in 531 when the Frankish kings Chlothar I and Theuderic I conquered her homeland. Taken captive, she was eventually compelled to marry Chlothar I in 540, becoming queen of the Franks. After enduring years of an unhappy marriage, exacerbated by Chlothar's murder of her brother, Radegund fled the court and, with the support of Bishop Medardus of Noyon, was consecrated as a deaconess, renouncing her royal status for a life of asceticism. In 558, she founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross in Poitiers, which she endowed with extensive lands and, most famously, a relic of the True Cross, obtained from the Byzantine Emperor Justin II, solidifying its spiritual prestige and her own.
